deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It contains no formulas, no computation and no derivation. It is a heavily reworked philosophical draft on causality, probably connected with Riemann's natural-philosophy fragments (the previous page quotes Newton's letter to Bentley against action at a distance). The argument has four numbered theses plus an epistemological paragraph. Several redrafts of the opening and a struck-out terminological digression are omitted below.

I. What an agens strives to bring about must be determined by the concept of the agens alone. Its action can depend on nothing other than its own essence (Wesen).

II. This requirement is met if the agens strives to preserve or restore itself (sich selbst zu erhalten oder herzustellen). Hence the agens must be variable in degree. Where such a striving exists and meets resistance, the agens will in fact be preserved or restored only 'as nearly as possible' (möglichst nahe).

III. Such an action is thinkable only if the agentia are not things but states of things or relations between things. The reasoning runs as follows:
- If a striving toward preservation or restoration occurs, it must be possible for it to be fulfilled inexactly. Where it conflicts with other actions, it will be fulfilled only approximately.
- So deviations of different degree from the target must be possible.
- But there are no degrees of being (keine Grade des Seins). Degree-wise deviation is thinkable only for states and relations.
- Therefore a self-preserving or self-restoring agens must be a state or a relation.

A crossed-out digression discusses how to render actio / effectus in German ('Wirkung' is ambiguous) and the phrase actio aequalis est reactioni ('die Kraft ist gleich der Gegenkraft'). Riemann proposes speaking of what an agens 'strives to bring about' (zu bewirken strebt).

IV. An action of states or relations can occur only on things capable of the same state or relation. On which of these things it acts, and whether it acts at all, cannot be read off from the concept of the agens.

Final paragraph (several drafts). The positive point is that analysing the concept of a thing cannot show that it is the cause of something else, so the causal concept is not analytic. The person criticised 'throws out the baby with the bathwater' (schüttet das Kind mit dem Bade aus) by later reducing the causal concept to a mere rule of temporal succession. This is the regularity view, which points to Hume rather than Kant as the target; one draft also invokes Kant's comparison with the concept of space. Riemann's own position is that even if causal necessity must be taken from experience, we may not renounce correcting and completing our conception of these empirical facts.

Modern gloss (mine, interpretive only). The 'self-restoring state that is realised only as nearly as possible when in conflict with other actions' is reminiscent of a restoring tendency dx/dt = -k(x - x0). Competing restoring tendencies then settle at a compromise equilibrium; for quadratic tendencies this is a weighted mean. This is a heuristic analogy, not Riemann's text.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible since there is no computation. Philosophically, the step 'no degrees of being, hence the agens must be a state or relation' is asserted rather than argued, as Riemann himself seems to sense through the many redrafts.

Which philosopher is meant in the final paragraph is ambiguous in the drafts. Reducing the causal concept to a 'bloße Regel der Zeitfolge' is Hume's position. Kant's Second Analogy also ties causality to the rule of temporal order, but Kant is not normally said to have 'thrown out' causal necessity.

results.what: Agentia (causes) are states or relations of things that strive to preserve or restore themselves, realised only approximately in conflict with other actions; things cannot be agentia because there are no degrees of being.
results.modern_name: Self-restoring-state conception of physical action (a precursor of field / equilibrium-tendency ontologies; cf. Herbart's Selbsterhaltung)
results.usually_credited_to: Herbart (self-preservation of 'Reale' against disturbance); field-ontology ideas to Faraday/Maxwell; Riemann's own version appears in his posthumously published natural-philosophy fragments

results.what: Critique of the regularity theory: causation is not analytic, yet reducing it to a rule of temporal succession throws out the baby with the bathwater; empirical conceptions of causal necessity must remain open to correction.
results.modern_name: Critique of Humean regularity theory of causation
results.usually_credited_to: Hume (non-analyticity, regularity view); Kant (synthetic a priori reply)

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely philosophical draft material on causality in Riemann's known natural-philosophy vein, Herbart-influenced and anti-action-at-a-distance. Closely related ideas appear in his published 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts'. There is no mathematical content, and nothing here would be novel to historians.

checkable.sympy: x,k,x0,t,c=symbols('x k x0 t c'); f=Function('f'); dsolve(Eq(f(t).diff(t),-k*(f(t)-x0)),f(t))
checkable.asserts: Interpretive illustration only (not in the manuscript): a state striving to restore itself, dx/dt=-k(x-x0), relaxes exponentially to x0, i.e. f(t)=x0+C*exp(-k*t).

checkable.sympy: a,b,x1,x2,x=symbols('a b x1 x2 x'); solve(diff(a*(x-x1)**2+b*(x-x2)**2,x),x)
checkable.asserts: Interpretive illustration only: two conflicting quadratic restoring tendencies settle at x=(a*x1+b*x2)/(a+b), so each target is attained only 'as nearly as possible'.

transcription_corrections: 'erschüttert den Hume mit dem Grunde aus' / 'schüttelt den Hume mit dem Grunde nicht' is almost certainly the idiom 'schüttet das Kind mit dem Bade aus' (throws the baby out with the bathwater).

The final paragraph's lead-in, transcribed as 'Diese richtige Bemerkung Kants', more plausibly reads 'Sehr richtig bemerkte Hume' (or similar). The object of criticism ('er', who reduced causality to a mere rule of temporal succession) fits Hume; a struck variant begins 'Wie Hume bemerkt hat'. One draft line may genuinely mention Kant's comparison with the concept of space.
'Wird des Falls, wenn das agens...' should read 'Diese Forderung wird genügt, wenn das agens sich selbst zu erhalten oder herzustellen strebt' (the interlinear addition replaces the struck start).

Thesis IV probably reads: 'Auf welche von diesen Dingen sie aber stattfindet, und ob sie stattfindet, kann aus dem Begriffe des Agens nicht ersehen/bestimmt werden', not 'Auf welche weiter diese Dingen ... gestattet werden'.

'Diese Darstellung anderer Darstellungen widerspricht' is doubtful. The interlinear words above 'dem Grade nach verschiedene' seem to concern deviations ('Abweichungen') of states and relations, not 'Darstellungen'.
'So gewiss wir die Causalnothwendigkeit aus der Erfahrung entnehmen müssten' may contain a negation in the original ('nicht ... entnehmen können'); this should be checked against the image.
